_comment: Twelve canonical shopping intents, each written three or four ways.
The property under test is the one `demand-intent.ts` claims in its header:
word order and punctuation cannot create a second intent, because word order
never reaches the aggregate. Every variant in a group is the same request
phrased differently — reordered, capitalised, punctuated, possessive or not —
and the group passes only when all of its variants canonicalise to a single
`DemandIntent`.
`triple` is scored alongside it and is deliberately the WEAKER measure. The
semantic triple carries the raw colour term and the brand as parsed, so
'grey' and 'gray' split it while both map to the same colour family — which
is exactly why the family mapping exists. Reporting both makes the
difference visible instead of arguable.
Two variants are annotated knowing the parser disagrees, and both stay:
ci-08b  'linen shirt light blue' — the head-noun rule is head-position
only, so with the colour trailing, the class comes back null and
the intent splits from its own group.
ci-12b  'cargo trousers olive' — 'cargo' is read as a leading-run brand.
The intent still canonicalises, because a guessed brand is refused
at the aggregate; only the triple splits. That refusal is the
single most important line in `demand-intent.ts` and this is the
case that exercises it.
`known` is the brand lexicon the parse is given. Three names, all real
labels carried by the licensed feed, none of them a user's words.
